facts.raw_span: A 30-year-old man
asymptomatic, calcified mass on the right anterior maxilla
had been present for 18 months
mucosal fenestration through which a hard, mineralized structure approximately 1 cm in diameter was visible
periapical radiograph of the upper right premolar area demonstrated a discrete radiopaque lesion
initial diagnostic hypothesis was maxillary exostosis
incisional biopsy was performed to remove a fragment of the lesion
submitted for histopathological analysis

concepts.why: The presence of a calcified mass on the right anterior maxilla, a mucosal fenestration with a hard mineralized structure, and a discrete radiopaque lesion on the periapical radiograph support the diagnosis of maxillary exostosis.
The mineralized structure and the discrete radiopaque lesion are consistent with a compound odontoma, a type of odontogenic tumor.
The asymptomatic mass and the discrete radiopaque lesion are consistent with a periosteal osteoma, a type of bony tumor.
The presence of a calcified mass and a mucosal fenestration with a hard mineralized structure support the diagnosis of a fibro-osseous lesion.
The mineralized structure and the discrete radiopaque lesion are consistent with a dental follicular hamartoma, a type of hamartomatous lesion.
The asymptomatic mass and the discrete radiopaque lesion are consistent with a maxillary osteoma, a type of bony growth.
The presence of a calcified mass and a mucosal fenestration with a hard mineralized structure support the diagnosis of a cemento-ossifying fibroma.
The mineralized structure and the discrete radiopaque lesion are consistent with an odontogenic keratocyst, a type of keratocystic odontogenic tumor.

rationales.F04: The mucosal fenestration and hard, mineralized structure are more characteristic of maxillary exostosis and cemento-ossifying fibroma.
rationales.F05: The discrete radiopaque lesion on the periapical radiograph is consistent with maxillary exostosis, compound odontoma, and cemento-ossifying fibroma.
rationales.F06: The initial diagnostic hypothesis of maxillary exostosis provides strong evidence for this condition.
